fixes.explanation: Paul goes the other direction, friend. He writes, "…we try to persuade men." You can't persuade somebody you're hiding from. Avoiding people is what a junk drawer is good for, and I would know. Paul says they try to persuade people.

Paul writes that some take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. Appearances are like a cookie that looks perfect on top and is raw dough in the middle. Pretty on the outside, nothing going on inside. Paul wants the Corinthians to be able to answer them.

Money never comes up in this verse, friend. Paul says some take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. Appearances are what you can see from across the room. The heart is what Paul sets against that.

Paul writes, "if we are of sound mind, it is for you." The "you" is the church in Corinth, the people he's writing to (2 Corinthians 1:1). So being out of their mind is for God, and being of sound mind is for the Corinthians. I think that's a pretty generous way to describe your own behavior.
Paul writes, "…Christ’s love compels us…" Compels is a strong word, like being pressed to act. I think that's the difference between a job you're handed and being moved by Christ's love.

Paul writes, "Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer." So there was a time they regarded Christ according to the flesh. Now they don't. That's a real change in how they see Him.

Prayers are good, friend, but they're not in this verse. It says God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, "…not counting men’s trespasses against them." Trespasses are wrongs people have done, and those are what God wasn't counting. That's the part worth sitting with.

Vows are promises people make, friend, and they don't appear in this verse. Paul writes that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, "…not counting men’s trespasses against them." Trespasses are wrongs people have done, and those are what God wasn't counting. I'd stay on those two words, not counting, a little longer.

Grateful sounds sweet, friend, but Paul's word is different. He writes, "We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God." Earlier he says God "reconciled us to Himself through Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:18). So reconciled is the word for what God has done, and Paul implores people to be reconciled to Him.

Paul writes, "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." Read it slowly and you see the two sides. The One who knew no sin was made to be sin on our behalf. The purpose is that "in Him we might become the righteousness of God." That's the text's reason, and I'll leave it as big as Paul wrote it.

Paul writes, "…we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain." In vain means for nothing, like getting handed a fresh batch of cookies and letting them go stale on the counter. I think Paul wants the grace to count for something.
That's not what Paul warns about, friend. He writes, "…we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain." Outsiders aren't mentioned in this verse. The warning is about receiving it in vain.
